global-wind-patterns-s2.title: Average yearly precipitation by latitude band

plot.label: Bar chart of average yearly precipitation in five latitude bands of the Northern Hemisphere, invented data

items.q: What sets global winds in motion in the first place?
options: The Sun heats the equator more than the poles
The Moon's gravity pulls the air toward the equator
Mountains push air up wherever they stand
Ocean waves drag the air along with them

why.correct: Uneven heating makes warm, light air rise near the equator and cooler, denser air sink elsewhere. The air moving between them is wind.
options: Right: unequal heating drives air to rise in some places and sink in others.
The Moon drives tides, not the global winds.
Mountains steer and lift wind locally, but they do not start global circulation.
Waves are made by wind, not the other way around.

items.q: Why do the trade winds in the Northern Hemisphere blow from the northeast instead of straight from the north?
options: Earth's rotation turns moving air to the right
The rising Sun in the east pushes the air west
Mountains along the equator turn the wind to the west
Warm air at the equator pulls the wind toward it from the east

why.correct: Air flowing toward the equator is deflected by Earth's rotation, the Coriolis effect: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, so a north wind becomes a northeast wind.
options: Right: the Coriolis effect turns the wind to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Sunlight heats air; it does not push it west.
There is no continuous mountain range along the equator.
Air at the equator rises; it draws air in from the north and south, and the turn comes from rotation.

items.q: Which way does the Coriolis effect deflect moving air in the Southern Hemisphere?
options: To the left of its direction of motion
To the right of its direction of motion
Straight up, away from the ground
It does not deflect air south of the equator

why.correct: Moving air is turned to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, which is why the southern trade winds blow from the southeast.
options: Right: deflection is to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
Rightward deflection is the Northern Hemisphere pattern.
The Coriolis effect turns air sideways, not upward.
It acts in both hemispheres; only the direction of turning differs.

items.q: Many of the world's large deserts, such as the Sahara, lie near 30° N or 30° S. Why?
options: Dry air sinks there and warms, so clouds rarely form
The trade winds blow sand from the equator to 30°
Those latitudes receive the most direct sunlight
Rising air there cools and drops its rain out at sea

why.correct: Air that rose at the equator dropped its rain there. It sinks near 30°, warming as it falls, so it can hold more water and clouds rarely form.
options: Right: sinking, warming air makes the 30° latitudes dry.
Trade winds carry air, not most of the sand in the Sahara.
The most direct sunlight falls near the equator.
Air sinks at 30°; it rises near the equator and near 60°.

items.q: Tropical rainforests are found near the equator. How do global wind patterns help explain this?
options: Warm, moist air rises there and cools into rain
Cold air sinks at the equator and brings steady rain
The westerlies carry rain from the poles to the equator
Air at the equator stays still, so rain falls straight down

why.correct: Strong heating makes air rise near the equator. As it rises it cools, and its water vapor condenses into clouds and heavy rain.
options: Right: rising air at the equator brings heavy rain.
Air rises at the equator; sinking air is dry.
The westerlies blow between about 30° and 60°, not toward the equator.
Air at the equator rises strongly; it is far from still.

items.q: Put the steps of the Hadley cell in order, starting at the equator.
options: Air is heated at the equator and rises
Rising air cools and drops rain
Dry air spreads toward the poles high up
Air sinks near 30° and warms
Air flows back toward the equator along the surface as the trade winds

why.correct: The loop: heat, rise, rain, spread poleward aloft, sink near 30°, return along the surface as the trade winds.

items.q: In the diagram, which winds blow at the surface between about 30° N and 60° N?
options: The westerlies
The northeast trade winds
The polar easterlies
The southeast trade winds

why.correct: Between 30° and 60° the surface winds blow from the west toward the east: the westerlies. They carry weather across most of the United States from west to east.
options: Right: the westerlies blow between 30° and 60°.
The trade winds blow between the equator and 30°.
The polar easterlies blow poleward of 60°.
The southeast trade winds are in the Southern Hemisphere, between the equator and 30° S.

items.q: The diagram shows air rising at both the equator and 60°, and sinking at 30° and the poles. Which statement explains the pattern of wet and dry places it labels?
options: Rising air cools and makes rain; sinking air warms and dries
Sinking air cools and makes rain; rising air warms and dries
Places with rising air get less sunlight, so they stay wet
Sinking air carries water down from the upper air as rain

why.correct: Rising air expands and cools, so its water vapor condenses into clouds and rain. Sinking air is compressed and warms, so clouds evaporate.
options: Right: rising means rain, sinking means dry.
The pattern is reversed: rising air cools, sinking air warms.
The equator gets the most sunlight and is very wet.
Air high up is dry; sinking air brings no rain.

items.q: A sailing ship leaves Spain (about 40° N) and heads for the Caribbean (about 15° N). According to the diagram, which winds should it use for the long crossing west?
options: The northeast trade winds, after sailing south to below 30° N
The westerlies, staying at 40° N the whole way
The polar easterlies, after sailing north of 60° N
The southeast trade winds, after crossing the equator

why.correct: The trade winds blow from the east, toward the west, between about 30° N and the equator. Sailing ships went south first to catch them, which is how they got their name.
options: Right: the northeast trades push ships west below 30° N.
The westerlies blow toward the east, against a ship sailing west.
Going north of 60° is far out of the way, and the Caribbean is in the tropics.
The Caribbean is north of the equator, so crossing it is not needed.

items.q: Smoke from large fires in the western United States, near 40° N, often drifts over the eastern states days later. Which feature in the diagram explains this?
options: The westerlies carry air east at these latitudes
The trade winds carry air from west to east at these latitudes
The Hadley cell lifts the smoke high over the equator
The polar easterlies push the smoke south and east

why.correct: Between about 30° and 60° N the prevailing winds are the westerlies, so smoke, dust and storms usually move from west to east across North America.
options: Right: the westerlies move air eastward across the middle latitudes.
The trade winds blow from east to west, and only between the equator and 30°.
The Hadley cell lies between the equator and 30°.
The polar easterlies blow north of 60°.

items.q: Which latitude band in the graph gets the most precipitation?

why.correct: The 0-10° N bar is tallest, at 2,000 mm per year, where air rises near the equator.
options: Right: the band near the equator is the wettest.
20-30° N gets 450 mm, one of the driest bands, where air sinks.
40-60° N gets 1,000 mm, half as much as near the equator.
60-80° N gets 350 mm, the least.

items.q: Use the graph. How many times more precipitation falls in the 0-10° N band than in the 20-30° N band? Give your answer to one decimal place.

why.correct: $\frac{2{,}000\,\text{mm}}{450\,\text{mm}} \approx 4.4$ times. The mm cancel, so the answer has no unit.

mistakes.why: You divided the smaller value by the larger. "How many times more" puts the larger value on top: 2,000 ÷ 450.
That is how many more millimeters, not how many times more. Divide: 2,000 ÷ 450.

items.q: Which pattern of air motion matches the shape of the graph?
options: Rising air near 0° and 60°, sinking air near 30°
Sinking air near 0° and 60°, rising air near 30°
Rising air at each of the latitudes
Sinking air near 0°, rising air near the poles

why.correct: Precipitation is high near the equator, low near 30°, higher again from 40-60° and low near the poles: wet where air rises, dry where it sinks.
options: Right: wet bands match rising air and dry bands sinking air.
This is reversed; sinking air brings dry weather.
Then every band would be wet, but 20-30° and 60-80° are dry.
The equator band is the wettest, which needs rising air there.

items.q: A student concludes from the graph that places farther from the equator always get less rain. Is this conclusion supported?
options: No: the 40-60° N band gets more rain than the 20-30° N band
Yes: each band is drier than the band closer to the equator
Yes: the 60-80° N band is the driest band on the graph
No: the 0-10° N band gets less rain than the 10-20° N band

why.correct: Rain falls from 2,000 to 450 mm by 20-30° N, then rises to 1,000 mm at 40-60° N before falling again. The pattern is not a steady decline.
options: Right: rainfall rises again in the middle latitudes.
The 40-60° N band (1,000 mm) is wetter than the 20-30° N band (450 mm).
The driest band does not show a steady decline; the middle of the graph rises.
0-10° N gets 2,000 mm, more than 10-20° N (1,100 mm).

items.q: Explain why the area near 30° N is dry, starting from the heating at the equator.

why.correct: Every link is needed: heating, rising and rain at the equator, dry air moving poleward aloft, and sinking, warming air near 30°.

specific.frame: Air heated at the equator ___, then ___, so near 30° N ___.

first.label: At the equator
options: rises, cools and drops its rain
sinks and warms
stays still and absorbs water

why.1: Heated air is light, so it rises; it does not sink at the equator.
why.2: Heated air rises; it does not stay still.

then.label: Next
options: the dry air moves toward the poles high up
the moist air flows north along the ground
the air freezes into ice in the upper air

why.1: At the surface near 30° the trade winds flow toward the equator, not away from it.
why.2: The air does not freeze into ice; it moves poleward.

result.label: Near 30° N
options: the air sinks and warms, so clouds rarely form
the air rises and makes heavy rain
the air cools and makes snow

why.1: Air sinks near 30°; rising air near 30° would make rain.
why.2: Sinking air warms; it does not cool.

specific.model: Air heated at the equator rises, cools and drops its rain, then the dry air moves toward the poles high up, so near 30° N it sinks and warms, which causes clouds to evaporate and leaves the land dry.
